title: The highest rung
hook: a loan, a partnership or a job, so the person needn't ask again
carry: so they never need to ask

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maimonides' ladder of giving, and your line: the eight rungs. Which rung did you catch yourself on, and did you step up? Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

A heavy load starts to slip off a donkey's back. One person, walking alongside, can reach up and steady it. Easy. But wait until it crashes to the ground, and even a group of people will struggle to lift it back. That picture comes from Rashi, drawing on older teaching, in his commentary on a verse in Leviticus about a brother who is starting to fall into poverty. Catch it early, they say. Maimonides builds the top of his ladder of giving on that same verse. Today we climb to the highest rung.
screen: `A LOAD BEGINS TO SLIP.` → `ONE PERSON CAN STEADY IT.` → `ONCE IT FALLS, IT'S HARD TO LIFT.`

segments.voice: The highest rung. Here is how Maimonides describes it, in plain English: the greatest level, above which there is none, is to strengthen the hand of someone who has become poor. Give them a gift or a loan, or go into partnership with them, or find them work. Strengthen their hand until they don't need to ask anyone. Turn it four ways. First, the verse. Leviticus says, when your brother grows poor and his hand falters beside you, uphold him. In Hebrew, v'hechezakta bo: strengthen him, hold him firm. Maimonides echoes it: strengthen their hand. Second, the list. Look at what counts as top-rung giving. A gift, yes. But also a loan, which comes back. A partnership, where both people stand to gain. A job. None of these looks much like charity. Some of them might even look like business. Maimonides puts them at the top. Third, the aim. Every lower rung relieves a need. This one ends it. The goal is not that the person feels grateful to you, but that they no longer need you, or anyone. A good gift, at this height, works itself out of a job. Fourth, the timing. Remember the donkey. The verse speaks of someone whose hand is only beginning to falter. The highest rung often comes before the fall: the loan that keeps a shop open, the introduction that lands someone work, the partner who shares the risk. It can look ordinary. It might not feel like giving at all. That may be part of why it sits so high. The person helped keeps their dignity, and walks on.
screen: `STRENGTHEN THEIR HAND.` · `A GIFT, A LOAN, A PARTNER, A JOB.` · `END THE NEED, NOT JUST EASE IT.` · `CATCH THE LOAD BEFORE IT FALLS.` · then, large: `SO THEY NEVER NEED TO ASK.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to help someone become independent. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person whose hand is faltering a little. A friend looking for work. A neighbor learning something new. A younger colleague. Now ask, gently, what would strengthen their hand, rather than carry them? An introduction. A skill you could teach. A reference. Picture yourself offering it, without making a fuss. Let one concrete step become clear. Then rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
The highest rung. In Maimonides' ladder, strengthening someone with a gift, a loan, a partnership or a job, so they won't need to ask anyone. Today's word.
Your line: so they never need to ask. Today, take one small step that helps someone stand on their own, a name, a skill, a word to the right person. Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Jewish communities run interest-free loan funds, each called a gemach, and Hebrew Free Loan societies, along with job and business help, as ways of giving at the highest rung.

fork.setup: a friend's small business is slipping. they haven't asked you for anything yet. what would put you on the highest rung?
options: wait until they ask, then give generously.
offer a loan or a partnership that keeps the business standing.
give them some money now, quietly.
fork.reveal: Maimonides' top rung is strengthening the person's hand, by gift, loan, partnership or job, so they won't need to ask anyone.

original.note: Hebrew: and you shall uphold him, from Leviticus 25:35, the verse Maimonides builds the top rung on.

trapdoor: what you thought: the best giving is the biggest giving.
what it means: the best giving makes the gift unnecessary: a loan, partnership or job so they won't need to ask.
what a scholar hears: Matanot Aniyim 10:7, grounded in Leviticus 25:35, with Rashi's image of the load steadied on the donkey before it falls.

notes: Matanot Aniyim 10:7 paraphrased. Leviticus 25:35 paraphrased because the exact JPS 1917 wording ('then thou shalt uphold him' vs 'then shalt thou uphold him') was not certain.
The donkey image is Rashi on Leviticus 25:35 (from the Sifra); the number of people in Rashi's version is deliberately omitted. Please confirm the attribution 'the old commentators'.
howItsDone mentions gemach funds and Hebrew Free Loan societies; please confirm.
'That may be part of why it sits so high' is offered as interpretation, not as Maimonides' stated reason; please confirm.

Editor: 'the old commentators' became 'Rashi, drawing on older teaching' (Rashi after the Sifra), and the myth answer follows; cut 'the verb is about grip, not about handouts', a word-root claim no cited text makes.
